extracted.intended_audience: readers and critics of political/economic pamphlets; policymakers and ministers evaluating fiscal proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and critique public fiscal and political reform proposals, focusing on the soundness of estimates, feasibility of savings/revenues, and prudence of policy measures. The rubric centers on what a proposer must show to make a credible plan for public finance and national defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in rhetorical framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not exhibit alarming prospects to the public if they are not true, nor present false horrors; a mind not devoid of feeling cannot view such prospects without horror, and an honest man should not exhibit them if false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dramatize or invent catastrophic scenarios to justify proposals; avoid terrifying descriptions unless supported by evidence. The author argues that displaying such prospects without truth is either indiscreet or dishonest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasons for estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Any estimate (e.g., of a peace establishment) must be justified with reasons and data; an estimate is the groundwork of any plan and 'ought to be well and firmly laid, or what must become of the superstructure?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than presenting figures alone, show how each article of expenditure was derived and why changes (increases or decreases) are warranted; compare article-by-article with existing estimates and explain deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base reforms on existing, practicable estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural method is to take present existing estimates as they stand and then show what may be practicably and safely defalcated from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground proposals in current realities rather than idealized or obsolete schemes; demonstrate what parts of current spending are practically reducible without endangering services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and coherence of accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not decrease overall cost by simultaneously claiming both reductions and unexplained increases; reductions should not be mere arithmetic tricks—'he is able to diminish by increasing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure internal consistency: if a head is reduced in one place and raised in another, explain the rationale. Avoid presenting numbers that contradict earlier principles or estimates without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify what will be cut, not just totals
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing savings (particularly on defence services), state what branch, work, or stores are considered superfluous rather than offering generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, for naval savings, specify which naval force elements, works, and stores could be dispensed with and over what reasonable term; do not simply state an aggregate cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider long-term and irregular charges
rubrics_metrics.description: A single year's estimate is no just idea of a permanent peace establishment; many charges (e.g., stockpiling hemp, large works) intermit but do not end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess permanent requirements over a reasonable multi-year horizon and account for intermittent but necessary expenditures; base 'permanent' savings on durable adjustments, not one-off timing effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate economy with arbitrary defalcation
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy should not be arbitrary trimming of charges that are necessary for defence or public service—'I will never suffer the sacred name of economy to be bestowed upon arbitrary defalcation of charge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine efficiencies and harmful cuts; avoid calling any cut 'economy' if it undermines essential capability or safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence for reductions in extraordinaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to reduce extraordinaries (e.g., army and ordnance extras) should be supported by concrete evidence, not mere assertion; on American extraordinaries one cannot 'cut down this bill... at his pleasure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain operational changes, force dispositions, or administrative reforms that would materially reduce extraordinaries and show likely magnitudes rather than relying on wishful thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not cherry-pick favorable years for statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: A prudent financier should not select a favorable year or two at remote periods to ground calculations; instead use reasonable recent averages or the lowest mediums to allow for unforeseen defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral, representative data (e.g., mediums of immediately preceding years) and adopt conservative assumptions. Avoid basing long-term policy on anomalous short-term figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish time-based savings from administration-made savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Savings that arise solely from the passage of time (e.g., apprenticeships ending, one-off surveys) cannot be counted as part of a new administration's plan of economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming savings, indicate whether they are contingent on administrative action or are simply the natural expiration of prior commitments; only include the former as attributable to policy change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fully analyze jurisdictions before proposing taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not propose new taxes in a country with which one is not personally conversant without laying open its situation minutely and critically (trade, remittances, exchange, establishments, debts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct a comprehensive fiscal and economic analysis of the affected jurisdiction; do not generalize from a single trade branch or isolated statistic when proposing taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify levy and collection mechanisms for colonial taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: If claiming colonial revenue, explain how it will be levied, in what proportion across diverse colonies, and what enforcement mechanisms exist; leaving mode to assemblies or vague propositions is ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete plans for assessment, apportionment among colonies with varied circumstances, and collection/enforcement; consider local valuation methods (e.g., land valued in gross) and administrative feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing plans on speculative revenues or inducements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on hopes, 'might be induced', expectations, or insinuations (e.g., inducing America and Ireland to pay) as firm revenue — speculative inducements are not dependable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat speculative sources as contingent and provide fallback plans; quantify risks and avoid counting uncertain inducements as firm credit for large budgetary commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about what revenues are and their realizability
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigning revenue figures (e.g., American revenue £200,000; Ireland £100,000), specify on what articles, by what means, and at what expense they will be collected — 'if supply is to be got in such a manner, farewell the lucrative mystery of finance!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide itemized revenue bases, collection costs, anticipated compliance, and realistic realizability assessments rather than bare headline numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure robustness; do not hinge success on a single person or chance
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan that depends on the author's personal power, permanence in office, success of projects, and life is fragile — 'ultimately all hangs on his life'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design policies robust to changes in personnel and political fortunes; avoid making national salvation contingent on improbable confluence of favorable events tied to a single individual.
